oneSentence: The share of flagged results that are actually correct positives.
plainExplanation:
Precision looks only at the items a system marked as positive. It asks: out of those flagged items, how many were truly the thing we were looking for?

The input is a set of predictions and the real outcomes. For each case, the system either flags it as positive or does not. Then we compare those flags with reality.

A true positive means the system flagged something and it really was positive. A false positive means the system flagged something but it was not actually positive. Precision uses these two counts: true positives divided by all flagged positives.

So precision tells you how trustworthy a positive result is. High precision means few false alarms among the positives. It does not tell you how many real positives were missed; that is recall, a different measure.

everydayAnalogy.title: The blurry-photo folder
everydayAnalogy.story: A phone places 10 photographs in a folder labelled “blurry”. On inspection, 8 are genuinely blurry and 2 are clear photographs taken in low light. The phone’s precision for that folder is 8 out of 10, or 80%. This says nothing about blurry photographs left elsewhere in the gallery.

visual.title: Precision and false alarms
visual.learningObjective: After using this explainer, a reader should be able to say that precision measures how many flagged positives are actually correct, and how it changes when false positives rise or fall.
visual.description: An interactive panel shows a grid of cases split into true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives. Users adjust a threshold and class balance, then watch the predicted-positive group change and see precision update as a fraction and percentage.

steps.label: Start with the full set
steps.explanation: The screen shows all cases, with colours indicating what is truly positive or truly negative before any prediction threshold is applied.
steps.visualInstruction: Render a labelled grid or dot plot of cases. Use one colour family for true positives/false negatives and another for true negatives/false positives. Include a visible total count.

steps.label: Apply the threshold
steps.explanation: Moving the threshold changes which cases the system flags as positive. The predicted-positive group is outlined so the reader can see which items count in the precision calculation.
steps.visualInstruction: Provide a threshold slider. As it moves, animate or update an outline around all predicted positives. Keep counts for TP and FP visible beside the graphic.

steps.label: Read the precision formula
steps.explanation: A live formula updates: precision = true positives divided by all predicted positives, which is true positives plus false positives.
steps.visualInstruction: Display TP / (TP + FP) with the current numbers substituted and the percentage shown. Highlight false positives when they increase, to show why precision falls.

steps.label: Compare two settings
steps.explanation: The reader can switch between a stricter and a looser threshold to see the trade-off: fewer false alarms may improve precision, even if fewer total positives are found.
steps.visualInstruction: Add buttons for ‘stricter’ and ‘looser’ presets or allow side-by-side snapshots. Show the two precision values together for comparison.

visual.interaction: Users can move a threshold slider, switch class balance presets, and compare stricter versus looser settings while the counts and precision update immediately.
visual.accessibilityDescription: Screen-reader version: You are given a set of cases with real labels and system predictions. Precision is calculated from only the cases predicted positive. The explainer reports the current counts of true positives and false positives, then reads the formula precision equals true positives divided by true positives plus false positives. When the threshold becomes stricter, fewer cases are flagged positive. If false positives drop faster than true positives, precision rises. If many incorrect cases are flagged, precision falls.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: For reduced motion, show two static states instead of animation: one looser threshold and one stricter threshold. Each state lists counts for true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives, with the precision formula written out and the predicted-positive group clearly outlined.

workedExample.scenario: The procurement officer manually checks the product sheets flagged by the classifier as confirming both live captioning and keyboard navigation.
workedExample.input: The classifier flags 12 product sheets. Nine explicitly confirm both features. Three contain general accessibility language but do not confirm both requirements.
process: Count all flagged product sheets: 12 predicted positives.
Count the flagged sheets that confirm both required features: 9 true positives.
Count the flagged sheets that do not confirm both features: 3 false positives.
Calculate precision as TP divided by TP plus FP: 9 divided by 12, or 0.75.
workedExample.result: Precision is 75%. In other words, three quarters of the classifier's positive flags were correct. The calculation does not reveal how many product sheets confirming both features were left unflagged.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: At a UN Country Team working group, a procurement officer is finalising the accessibility requirements in the concept note for a side event in the margins of the session. With clearance due by close of business, the officer tests a classifier that screens event-platform product sheets for explicit confirmation of live captioning and keyboard navigation, rather than a general claim that the platform is accessible.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: High precision means that most product sheets flagged for follow-up actually confirm both required features. It does not show how many suitable platforms the classifier missed. The figure applies to the decision threshold and document mix tested, and may change when either changes.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not upload bids, pricing, evaluation comments or other procurement-sensitive material to a tool that has not been approved for it. This could expose confidential commercial information and compromise the integrity of the procurement process.

whyItMatters: A system can look useful while still producing many false alarms. Precision helps you judge whether a positive result is trustworthy enough for your task, especially when acting on a wrong alert has costs.
whereYouMayHearIt: During a vendor demo to a procurement unit, when staff ask how many automated flags survive manual review

commonMisconceptions.misconception: High precision means the system finds most of the real positives.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Not necessarily. A system can be very selective, flag only a few cases, and get most of those right. That gives high precision but may miss many true cases, which is low recall.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Precision and accuracy are basically the same.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Accuracy looks at all predictions, both positive and negative. Precision looks only at predicted positives, so it is often more informative when positive flags trigger action.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If precision is 90%, then 90% of all items are positive.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Precision is about the quality of the flagged positive set, not the share of positives in the whole dataset.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: When the system says ‘this one is a match’, precision tells you how often that positive signal is correct.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: For binary classification, precision, also called positive predictive value, equals TP divided by TP plus FP. It measures the proportion of predicted positives that are true positives, and it depends on the decision threshold and the data distribution.

keyTakeaway: Precision is the share of positive flags that are correct. It does not measure how many real positives were missed, and it can change with the threshold or data being assessed.

quickCheck.question: A system flags 20 messages as urgent. Human review shows that 15 really are urgent and 5 are not. What is the precision?
quickCheck.explanation: Precision uses only flagged positives: true positives divided by all predicted positives. Here that is 15 divided by 20, which equals 75%. The unflagged messages do not enter this calculation.

issues.problem: The formula omits the zero-denominator case. If the system predicts no positives, TP + FP is zero and precision is undefined.
issues.fix: Precision, or positive predictive value, is TP divided by TP plus FP. It is undefined when no cases are predicted positive. Otherwise, it is the true-positive share of predicted positives and depends on the threshold and data distribution.

issues.problem: The interactive visual lets users adjust class balance, but the screen-reader version mentions only threshold changes. It therefore does not convey the same mechanism or explain that class balance can affect precision.
issues.fix: Screen-reader version: You are given cases with real labels and system predictions. Controls change the threshold and class balance. The explainer reports true positives and false positives, then reads precision as true positives divided by true positives plus false positives. A stricter threshold can reduce the number of flagged cases. Precision rises if false positives fall proportionally more than true positives. Changing the class balance can also change precision because the mix of true and false cases changes.
